title: The Chariot: Who Is Holding the Reins?
reflection: Once a day, especially in a hard moment, ask one question: who is holding the reins right now? Is there a steady you choosing, or have the horses taken the bit? Naming it is often enough to bring the charioteer half awake.

questions.q: In the chariot of the Kaṭha Upaniṣad, which part is the charioteer, and what is it?
o: Buddhi, the power of discernment and judgment that decides what matters and where to go.
Manas, the attention that turns toward this and then that, and so serves as the reins.
The senses, which pull toward all that is bright and loud and tasty on the road.
The Self, the awareness for whom the whole journey is made, who rides in the back.
questions.e: The body is the chariot, the senses the horses, objects the roads, manas the reins, buddhi the charioteer and the Self the rider. Chitta is the terrain, the ruts worn by years, and ahaṁkāra the I-maker who claims it all as mine.

questions.q: Kai says that most of the time his phone just runs him and there is no me deciding. How does Swamiji read it?
o: The hierarchy has flipped and the horses have taken over: a seating problem, not a flaw of character.
He is weak-willed, which is the common fault and may be mended by an effort of the will each day.
He is simply tired, so a good night’s sleep is all that is needed to put the whole matter right.
The phone is to blame, so he should give it up for good, since nothing else would change anything.
questions.e: Something bright flashes, the senses bolt, the reins are yanked out of the charioteer’s hands, and the command runs bottom-up. Kai’s honesty is the doorway. Seeing it as a seating problem lets you stop blaming the person.
questions.c: A flipped hierarchy is a seating problem

questions.q: “In a good moment, command runs from the top down: from judgment to attention, to the senses and to the body.”
questions.e: That is a life navigated. The same picture shows what practice trains: steadying attention strengthens the reins, cultivating discernment wakes the charioteer, and settling body and breath calms the horses. It is all chariot maintenance, and a good practice tends every part together.

questions.q: Dr Watson says ‘just decide to get up’ is useless and even cruel for a depressed patient. How does the chariot explain it?
o: The charioteer can still decide, but the horses lie down in the road, and willpower cannot raise them.
The patient does not wish to get up, and no one can make a person wish for what he does not want.
The charioteer has lost the reins altogether, so the patient is unable to decide on anything at all.
The road is too hard for any horse to travel, so the best course is to find an easier road to follow.
questions.e: Anxiety is the horses bolting: fast breath, pounding heart, no off-switch. Depression is the mirror: the energy drains, the senses go dull, nothing pulls. Both are the same inversion in opposite directions, and pull yourself together fails for a structural reason.
questions.c: Willpower cannot raise a collapsed horse

questions.q: What place does Swamiji give the breath in the chariot picture?
o: The one rein you can always reach, which calms the horses: first aid, not the journey home.
The whole road home, since the breath alone can steady the horses and wake the charioteer.
A rein of no use, since the horses can only be steadied by the will of the charioteer.
The charioteer himself, since the breath is what decides where the chariot is to be driven.
questions.e: Slow long out-breaths settle bolting horses; gentle energising breath and movement lift fallen ones. It buys a steadier moment. The lasting work is waking the charioteer and steadying it to a single point: one-pointedness, the work of the next module. Don’t mistake the first move for the whole road.
questions.c: Breath settles the horses; it is not the road

questions.q: “Breathwork is the whole of the path home, and nothing more is needed once the breath is steady.”
questions.e: Swamiji says breathwork is only a small part of the path. It calms the horses; the lasting work is waking the charioteer, the buddhi, and steadying it until it can hold the reins on its own and stay turned toward the Self riding behind.
questions.c: Breath is a small part of the path

questions.q: James has a child who is bolting and another who has lain down. What does Swamiji say he can offer?
o: The bolter needs a pause and a breath; the fallen one needs a small movement and a reachable task.
The same firm instruction to both, since a clear order is what every pupil needs to bring the horses back.
Nothing at all for either, since a pupil in this state cannot be reached until the state has passed.
A longer lesson for both, since more to do is the surest way to bring the attention back to the work.
questions.e: Settle the horses before any learning, and only then can the real work, attention steadying onto something worth holding, begin. The same reading serves a room, a patient or oneself: which way has the chariot gone wrong, what settles the horses, and what steadies the driver.
questions.c: Match the first move to the direction of the fall

questions.q: Kai pictures his exam anxiety: the worry arrives, the body floods, and each version of the disaster is stamped ‘my fault’. What does Swamiji say of the stamp?
o: The I-maker claims every spark and adds weight; noticing the tagging is half the freedom already.
The stamp is a true record of what he has done, and it ought to be heeded as a fair warning.
The stamp is of no importance, since the horses alone decide how the chariot is to be driven.
The stamp comes from the exam itself, so that it will pass of its own accord once the exam is over.
questions.e: Ahaṁkāra is the I-maker, the standing tilt of me and mine. In the anxious mind it claims every spark, which makes it heavier. In the depressed mind it goes rigid and grim, I am worthless, and the self-story nails the horses where they lie.

questions.q: A musician is lost in playing, hands flying, fully engaged and not anxious at all. How does the chariot read this?
o: Good order in motion: charioteer awake, reins firm, the horses galloping, so there is flow.
A mind that is out of order, since so much activity is a sign that the horses have taken over.
The same state as a deep meditation, in stillness, with the breath long and the hands at rest.
A state of no mind at all, since the musician is said to be unaware of himself as he plays.
questions.e: Good order is not only stillness. Years of practice make the chariot reliable even at full speed. So there are two ways the chariot fails, and two ways it works, one still and one moving. A noisy mind is not a broken mind but a misfitted one, and misfit can be refitted.
questions.c: Flow is good order in motion

questions.q: Sarah is asked to ask one question in a hard moment. What is it, and what is its use?
o: Who is holding the reins right now? Naming that the horses have it wakes the charioteer.
Who is to blame for this? Naming the one at fault often brings the hard moment to a quick end.
What should I do about it? Naming the best action often settles the matter at once and for good.
How long will this last? Naming the time it will take often lets her put up with it more easily.
questions.e: She does not have to fix it. This is the first lens, reading your own chariot, once a day. It would change her whole evening.
questions.c: Ask who is holding the reins
